Regularity of asymptotically axisymmetric solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with analytic forcing

Peter Constantin Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540 Email address: const@math.princeton.edu URL: https://web.math.princeton.edu/˜const/ , Mihaela Ignatova Address: Department of Mathematics, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA 19122 Email address: ignatova@temple.edu URL: https://sites.temple.edu/ignatova/ and Vlad Vicol Address: Department of Mathematics, Courant Institute, New York University, New York, NY, 10012 Email address: vicol@cims.nyu.edu URL: https://cims.nyu.edu/˜vicol/
Abstract.

OpenAI [43] has recently announced a proof of finite time singularity formation for the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, in the presence of a C∞C^{\infty}-smooth body force. The construction in [43] has a few key features, among which we single out: (i) the angular mean of the solution satisfies specific Type II bounds which are anisotropic; (ii) the solution is exactly axisymmetric in a collapsing core region. In this paper we consider solutions of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations in the presence of a real-analytic body force, and assume that these solutions satisfy properties (i) and (ii) above. We prove that such solutions are in fact regular at the putative singular point. As a consequence, in the construction of [43], and in any construction with properties (i) and (ii) whose force remains bounded in C2C^{2} up to the singular time, the force can neither vanish identically near the singular point, nor be real analytic in the space variables, locally uniformly in time. The main idea of the proof is inspired by our earlier work [13] and the companion paper [14]: zooming-in at the putative singularity using the anisotropic length scales provided by the a priori bounds, we arrive at ancient limits whose PDE evolution imposes additional rigidity.

Key words and phrases: 
Navier-Stokes equations, local regularity, axial symmetry, analytic forcing.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 35Q30; Secondary 35B44, 35Q31

1. Introduction

In a recent manuscript [43], OpenAI has announced a proof of finite time singularity formation for the 3D Navier-Stokes equations in the presence of a C∞C^{\infty}-smooth forcing. The main theorem of the manuscript [43, Theorem 1.1] asserts that for every viscosity ν>0\nu>0 there exists a force f∈Cc∞​(ℝ3×(0,∞))f\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(0,\infty)) and a smooth solution (u,π)(u,\pi) of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations on ℝ3×[0,1)\mathbb{R}^{3}\times[0,1)

∂tu+(u⋅∇)u−νΔu+∇π\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla\pi =f,\displaystyle=f\,,
div⁡u\displaystyle\operatorname{div}u =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
u⁡(⋅,0)\displaystyle u(\cdot,0) =0,\displaystyle=0\,,

which has a fixed compact spatial support, finite kinetic energy sup0≤t<1‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L2<∞\sup_{0\leq t<1}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}}<\infty, and the solution blows up as t↑1t\uparrow 1:

lim supt↑1‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞=∞.\limsup_{t\uparrow 1}\left\|u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}}=\infty\,.

We refer to the solution built in [43] as the OpenAI construction. The singular point is (x,t)=(0,1)(x,t)=(0,1), and it is isolated: the velocity diverges along points converging to the origin [43, equations (10.20)–(10.21)], while every space-time derivative of the velocity has a one-sided limit at the blowup time, on compact sets avoiding the origin; see [43, Theorem 3.1(ii), equation (3.5), and the proof of Lemma 10.2]. The force ff, in turn, is defined as the residual of the momentum equation, left over after the construction’s ansatz, and it is C∞C^{\infty} smooth but not real analytic: neither on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, because it is compactly supported, nor in the vicinity of the singular point (see Section A.6). In Appendix A we record those properties of the OpenAI construction which are relevant to this paper; they are deduced from statements of [43], which we cite with their locations.

Of the many features of the solution constructed in [43], we single out the two which enter the hypotheses of our main theorem:

  • (i)

    Near the singular point the angular mean v=𝒫​uv=\mathcal{P}u of the velocity, defined in (1.4) below, satisfies Type II bounds which are anisotropic: its radial component vrv_{r} is bounded by (1−t)−1/2(1-t)^{-1/2}, while its axial and azimuthal components vzv_{z} and vθv_{\theta} are bounded by (1−t)−1/2−h(1-t)^{-1/2-h} for some 0<h<1/1000<h<1/100. Moreover, each rr-derivative costs a factor of (1−t)−1/2(1-t)^{-1/2}, while each zz-derivative costs only a factor of (1−t)−1/2+h(1-t)^{-1/2+h}.

  • (ii)

    The full velocity field uu is exactly axisymmetric on a collapsing core region B⁡(c​1−t)B(c\sqrt{1-t}), for some c>0c>0 fixed.

We do not claim to have verified the correctness of the construction in [43]: Appendix A records the statements of that manuscript on which we rely, with their locations, and deduces from them the properties used in this paper.

1.1. Problem setup

The solution constructed in [43] is defined for t∈[0,1)t\in[0,1) and becomes singular as t↑1t\uparrow 1. Since the equations are invariant under translations in time, we place the singular time at t=0t=0, which is more convenient: we replace the triple (u,π,f)(u,\pi,f) of the manuscript [43] by the shifted functions

(1.1) (u,π,f)​(x,t)⟼(u,π,f)​(x,t+1),−1≤t<0.\displaystyle(u,\pi,f)(x,t)\longmapsto(u,\pi,f)(x,t+1)\,,\qquad-1\leq t<0\,.

We denote the shifted triple again by (u,π,f)(u,\pi,f). The singular point is then (x,t)=(0,0)(x,t)=(0,0), and the time to the singularity is −t-t, replacing the 1−t1-t in the time variable of [43]. In particular, the factor (1−t)(1-t) of item (i) becomes (−t)(-t), and the core of item (ii) becomes B⁡(c​−t)B(c\sqrt{-t}). From here on, every statement of this paper is in the shifted time coordinate of (1.1).

The goal of this paper is to analyze solutions of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations which are a priori assumed to obey properties (i) and (ii) above. We prove that if such solutions were to arise from the forced problem with a body force which is real analytic in the space variables, in the sense made precise in Theorem 1.1 below, then (x,t)=(0,0)(x,t)=(0,0) is a regular point.11 1 Recall that a point (x0,t0)(x_{0},t_{0}) with x0∈B⁡(1)x_{0}\in B(1) and −1<t0≤0-1<t_{0}\leq 0 is called regular if ess​supB⁡(x0,ρ)×(t0−ρ2,t0)⁡|u|<∞\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{B(x_{0},\rho)\times(t_{0}-\rho^{2},t_{0})}|u|<\infty for some ρ>0\rho>0 with B⁡(x0,ρ)×(t0−ρ2,t0)⊂B⁡(0,1)×(−1,0)B(x_{0},\rho)\times(t_{0}-\rho^{2},t_{0})\subset B(0,1)\times(-1,0), and singular otherwise. Here and throughout this paper, we use the notation B⁡(x,ρ)={y∈ℝ3:|y−x|<ρ}B(x,\rho)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:|y-x|<\rho\} and B⁡(ρ)=B⁡(0,ρ)B(\rho)=B(0,\rho).

Throughout the paper we consider suitable weak solutions, in the sense of Caffarelli, Kohn, and Nirenberg [6], of the forced 3D Navier-Stokes equations

(1.2a) ∂tu+(u⋅∇)u−Δu+∇π=f,\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\Delta u+\nabla\pi=f\,,
(1.2b) div⁡u=0,\displaystyle\operatorname{div}u=0\,,

where u:𝒬→ℝ3u\colon\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} is the velocity, π:𝒬→ℝ\pi\colon\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbb{R} is the pressure, and f:𝒬→ℝ3f\colon\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} is the force.22 2 The partial regularity results of [6] are stated for a divergence-free force. The function ∇πf\nabla\pi_{f} is bounded on B⁡(1)B(1) uniformly in time, so that f−∇πff-\nabla\pi_{f} is bounded and divergence free, and the local energy inequality is unchanged, since ∫u⋅∇(πf​φ)​𝑑x=0\int u\cdot\nabla(\pi_{f}\varphi)\,dx=0 for φ∈C0∞​(B⁡(1))\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(B(1)). Note that the definition of a suitable weak solution on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} in the sense of [6], as written in [40, 37], includes the integrability requirement

1.2. Notation

The solutions of (1.2) need not be axisymmetric, but it is convenient to introduce the notation attached to the cylindrical coordinate system on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. For φ∈[0,2​π)\varphi\in[0,2\pi), denote by QφQ_{\varphi} the rotation through angle φ\varphi about the zz-axis. For a solution u:𝒬→ℝ3u\colon\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} of (1.2) we define the rotation and the projection operators44 4 Since rotations about the zz-axis preserve B⁡(1)B(1), the angular mean projection operator 𝒫\mathcal{P} is well defined on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

(1.4a) (ℛφ​u)​(x,t)\displaystyle(\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}u)(x,t) =Qφ​u​(Qφ−1​x,t),𝒫​u=12​π​∫02​πℛφ​u​𝑑φ,\displaystyle=Q_{\varphi}u(Q_{\varphi}^{-1}x,t)\,,\qquad\mathcal{P}u=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}u\,d\varphi\,,
and denote
(1.4b) v=𝒫​u,w=u−v,𝒫​w=0.\displaystyle v=\mathcal{P}u\,,\qquad w=u-v\,,\qquad\mathcal{P}w=0\,.

We call vv the angular mean, or the axisymmetric part, of uu, and we refer to ww as the non-axisymmetric part. The field uu is axisymmetric if w=0w=0. With x=(x′,z)x=(x^{\prime},z), r=|x′|r=|x^{\prime}|, and the usual cylindrical frame (er,eθ,ez)(e_{r},e_{\theta},e_{z}), an axisymmetric field has the form u=ur​er+uθ​eθ+uz​ezu=u_{r}e_{r}+u_{\theta}e_{\theta}+u_{z}e_{z}, where ur,uθ,uzu_{r},u_{\theta},u_{z} depend only on (r,z,t)(r,z,t). For a general field uu, the cylindrical coefficients ur,uθ,uzu_{r},u_{\theta},u_{z} depend on θ\theta as well, and the cylindrical coefficients of its angular mean v=𝒫​uv=\mathcal{P}u are their averages in θ\theta, that is, v∘=12​π​∫02​πu∘​𝑑θv_{\circ}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}u_{\circ}\,d\theta for ∘∈{r,θ,z}\circ\in\{r,\theta,z\}.

1.3. Main result

Our main result is the following.

Theorem 1.1 (Regularity under anisotropic Type II bounds and analytic forcing).

Let (u,π)(u,\pi) be a suitable weak solution of (1.2) on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, smooth on compact subsets of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and let 0<h<1/20<h<1/2. Assume that the force is bounded in C2C^{2} up to the blowup time,

(1.5) Mf:=sup−1<t<0‖f⁡(⋅,t)‖Cx2​(B​(1))<∞.\displaystyle M_{f}:=\sup_{-1<t<0}\left\|f(\cdot,t)\right\|_{C_{x}^{2}(B(1))}<\infty\,.

Assume that the force is real analytic in the space variables, locally uniformly on cylinders compactly contained in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}: for every R<1R<1 and every compact interval J⊂(−1,0)J\subset(-1,0) there are MR,J<∞M_{R,J}<\infty and aR,J>0a_{R,J}>0 such that

(1.6) supt∈J‖∂xαf⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(R))≤MR,J​aR,J−|α|​|α|!for all ​α∈ℕ03.\displaystyle\sup_{t\in J}\left\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(R))}\leq M_{R,J}a_{R,J}^{-|\alpha|}|\alpha|!\qquad\mbox{for all }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{3}\,.

Assume that the velocity has the following two properties.

  1. (i)

    Its angular mean v:=𝒫​uv:=\mathcal{P}u satisfies, on the fixed Euclidean ball B⁡(1)B(1), for −1<t<0-1<t<0, and all nonnegative integers a,ba,b with a+b≤2a+b\leq 2,

    (1.7a) ‖∂ra∂zbvr​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))\displaystyle\|\partial_{r}^{a}\partial_{z}^{b}v_{r}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))} ≤𝖢axi(−t)−1/2−a/2−(1/2−h)b,\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}(-t)^{-1/2-a/2-(1/2-h)b}\,,
    (1.7b) ‖∂ra∂zbvz​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))+‖∂ra∂zbvθ​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B​(1))\displaystyle\|\partial_{r}^{a}\partial_{z}^{b}v_{z}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))}+\|\partial_{r}^{a}\partial_{z}^{b}v_{\theta}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(B(1))} ≤𝖢axi(−t)−1/2−h−a/2−(1/2−h)b,\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}(-t)^{-1/2-h-a/2-(1/2-h)b}\,,

    for a constant 𝖢axi>0\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}>0 which is independent of tt.

  2. (ii)

    For each t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0) there is a radius ρ⁡(t)∈(0,1)\rho(t)\in(0,1) such that the solution u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is exactly axisymmetric on the ball of radius ρ⁡(t)\rho(t); equivalently,

    (1.8) w⁡(⋅,t)=0on ​B​(ρ⁡(t)).\displaystyle w(\cdot,t)=0\qquad\mbox{on }B(\rho(t))\,.

    No regularity or quantitative lower bound is assumed on ρ\rho; we only need that ρ⁡(t)>0\rho(t)>0 at all t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0).

Then u=vu=v on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and (0,0)(0,0) is a regular point: there exist r∗,δ∗>0r_{*},\delta_{*}>0 such that

(1.9) supB⁡(r∗)×(−δ∗,0)|u|<∞.\displaystyle\sup_{B(r_{*})\times(-\delta_{*},0)}|u|<\infty\,.
Remark 1.2.

A few comments on the hypotheses of Theorem 1.1 are in order:

  • (a)

    The force assumptions (1.5) and (1.6) have distinct roles. Spatial analyticity (1.6) is used at each fixed time before the blowup time, so the analyticity radius aR,Ja_{R,J} is allowed to tend to zero as JJ approaches time 00.55 5 Condition (1.6) holds if and only if, for every R<1R<1 and every compact J⊂(−1,0)J\subset(-1,0), each f⁡(⋅,t)f(\cdot,t) with t∈Jt\in J is the restriction of a holomorphic function on a fixed complex neighborhood of B⁡(R)¯\overline{B(R)}, bounded uniformly in t∈Jt\in J. The regularity argument of Sections 3–5, which proves Theorem 1.3, uses instead the uniform spatial C2C^{2} bound (1.5). A force which is real analytic in (x,t)(x,t) on a neighborhood of B⁡(1)¯×[−1,0]\overline{B(1)}\times[-1,0] satisfies both conditions, and so does f=0f=0. No symmetry of ff is assumed, although, together with (1.8), the hypothesis (1.6) does make curl⁡f\operatorname{curl}f rotation invariant on all of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}; see Remark 2.5.

  • (b)

    The bounds (1.7) concern only the angular mean of the solution. Apart from the Lt∞​Lx2∩Lt2​Hx1​(𝒬)L^{\infty}_{t}L^{2}_{x}\cap L^{2}_{t}H^{1}_{x}(\mathcal{Q}) regularity implicit in the definition of a suitable weak solution, no bound on ww or its derivatives is assumed outside the core. The OpenAI construction does satisfy the bounds in (1.7); see Section A.3.

  • (c)

    The OpenAI construction satisfies (1.8) with ρ⁡(t)=c​−t\rho(t)=c\sqrt{-t}, for c>0c>0 a constant such that c<2​Xac<\sqrt{2X_{a}}; see Section A.2.

  • (d)

    The force used in [43] does not satisfy (1.6). This is consistent with the construction, whose force is built from compactly supported cutoffs.

  • (e)

    Exact axisymmetry on the core (1.8) and analyticity of the force (1.6) may be traded for an upper bound on the non-axisymmetric part of the velocity field. If ‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖C3​(B​(1))\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{C^{3}(B(1))} is bounded uniformly in t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0), then (0,0)(0,0) is regular. This statement requires no analyticity assumption at all; see Remark 2.4. The OpenAI construction does not satisfy such a bound on ww; see Section A.6.

1.4. From analytic forcing and axisymmetric core to an axisymmetric problem

Our first observation is that the analyticity assumption (1.6) on the force makes u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) real analytic on B⁡(1)B(1), for every fixed t∈(−1,0)t\in(-1,0). This follows from the classical interior analyticity theorem for the Navier-Stokes system, due to Kahane [32, Theorem 1.2 and p. 387]; we recall this result as Theorem 2.1, and Corollary 2.2 is the form in which we apply it. Combined with the axisymmetric core assumption (1.8), this makes uu axisymmetric on all of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}: for every rotation QφQ_{\varphi} about the zz-axis, the analytic field u−ℛφ​uu-\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}u vanishes on the core, hence on all of B⁡(1)B(1) by the identity theorem; these details are given in Section 2.2. Thus u=vu=v, and the bounds on the angular mean in (1.7) become bounds on the full velocity field. Once uu is known to be axisymmetric, we average (1.2) over the rotations ℛφ\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}, which leaves the velocity terms unchanged and replaces only the pressure and the force by their angular means. By (1.5), the angle-averaged force 𝒫​f\mathcal{P}f remains bounded in C2C^{2}.

This reduces Theorem 1.1 to the regularity of axisymmetric solutions of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with C2C^{2} forcing, under the anisotropic bounds inherited from (1.7). That result is Theorem 1.3 below, which is of independent interest. In order to state it, we fix the standing assumptions of Sections 3–5: (u,π)(u,\pi) is an axisymmetric suitable weak solution of the forced equations (1.2) on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, which is smooth on compact subsets of 𝒬\mathcal{Q},66 6 Smoothness in Cartesian coordinates gives ur=uθ=∂ruz=0u_{r}=u_{\theta}=\partial_{r}u_{z}=0 at r=0r=0, for all t<0t<0. in the class described in Section 1.1, and whose force satisfies (1.5). For 0<h<1/20<h<1/2 we define the radial and axial lengths as in [43]:

(1.10) ℓr​(t)=(−t)1/2,ℓz​(t)=(−t)1/2−h.\displaystyle\ell_{r}(t)=(-t)^{1/2}\,,\qquad\ell_{z}(t)=(-t)^{1/2-h}\,.

The range 0<h<1/20<h<1/2 ensures that both lengths tend to zero as t↑0t\uparrow 0. The bounds in (1.11) below are imposed on the scalar cylindrical coefficients of uu and on their derivatives through total order two, with each radial derivative costing a factor of ℓr−1\ell_{r}^{-1}, and each axial derivative costing a factor of ℓz−1\ell_{z}^{-1}. The following theorem is the anisotropic counterpart of the main result of [14]:

Theorem 1.3 (Regularity of axisymmetric solutions under anisotropic bounds).

Let (u,π)(u,\pi) be an axisymmetric suitable weak solution of (1.2) in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, which is smooth on compact subsets of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, with a force satisfying (1.5). Let 0<h<1/20<h<1/2. Suppose that there exists a constant 𝖢axi>0\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}>0 such that

(1.11a) |∂ra∂zbur​(r,z,t)|\displaystyle|\partial_{r}^{a}\partial_{z}^{b}u_{r}(r,z,t)| ≤𝖢axi(−t)−1/2−a/2−(1/2−h)b,\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}\,(-t)^{-1/2-a/2-(1/2-h)b}\,,
(1.11b) |∂ra∂zbuz​(r,z,t)|+|∂ra∂zbuθ​(r,z,t)|\displaystyle|\partial_{r}^{a}\partial_{z}^{b}u_{z}(r,z,t)|+|\partial_{r}^{a}\partial_{z}^{b}u_{\theta}(r,z,t)| ≤𝖢axi(−t)−1/2−h−a/2−(1/2−h)b,\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}\,(-t)^{-1/2-h-a/2-(1/2-h)b}\,,

on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, for all nonnegative integers a,ba,b with a+b≤2a+b\leq 2. Then, (0,0)(0,0) is a regular point.

Remark 1.4.

We make a few comments on the hypotheses of Theorem 1.3.

  • (a)

    The bounds in (1.11) say that the rescaled fields (−t)1/2​ur(-t)^{1/2}u_{r}, (−t)1/2+h​uz(-t)^{1/2+h}u_{z}, and (−t)1/2+h​uθ(-t)^{1/2+h}u_{\theta}, regarded as functions of (r/ℓr​(t),z/ℓz​(t))(r/\ell_{r}(t),z/\ell_{z}(t)), are bounded in C2C^{2} uniformly in tt; see (4.6) below.

  • (b)

    Neither (1.11) nor the Type I bound |u|≤C(−t)−1/2|u|\leq C(-t)^{-1/2} implies the other: at a=b=0a=b=0 the bounds on uzu_{z} and uθu_{\theta} in (1.11) are weaker by the factor (−t)−h(-t)^{-h}, while at every b≥1b\geq 1 the bound imposed on uru_{r} is smaller by the factor (−t)h​b(-t)^{hb} than the bound (−t)−1/2−(a+b)/2(-t)^{-1/2-(a+b)/2} which the parabolic scaling attaches to a Type I velocity bound. Theorem 1.3 is therefore not contained in the Type I results of Chen, Strain, Yau, and Tsai [7], Chen, Strain, Tsai, and Yau [8], Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin, and Šverák [33], or Seregin and Šverák [54], nor are those results contained in it.

  • (c)

    The proof of Theorem 1.3 may be completed using only the bounds on uru_{r} and uzu_{z} from (1.11), with the assumptions on uθu_{\theta} dropped altogether; see Remark 5.2. For cosmetic reasons, we nevertheless state (1.11) for the three components alike, and do not pursue the minimal hypothesis.

Next, we outline the proof of Theorem 1.3; the estimates and the full proof are postponed to Sections 3–5. The strategy is that of the companion paper [14], whose steps are as follows. In [14] we consider unforced axisymmetric solutions which are bounded in C2C^{2} after rescaling isotropically at a single vanishing length scale ℓ⁡(t)\ell(t), for which (−t)/ℓ​(t)2(-t)/\ell(t)^{2} tends to zero. Using this length scale we zoom in, along times and points at which the gradient of the meridional velocity is not small compared with (−t)−1(-t)^{-1}. Since the pressure is not controlled after such a zoom, the limit is taken in the vorticity equations rather than in the momentum equation. Partial regularity and the maximum principle bound the circulation r​uθru_{\theta} on a ball of fixed radius, and the rescaling multiplies it by a factor which vanishes, so that the swirl source of the potential vorticity equation disappears in the limit. The scalar carried into the limit is then either the potential vorticity or the azimuthal vorticity, depending on whether the rescaled axis stays at finite distance or recedes to infinity, and in both cases we prove that the limiting scalar vanishes at the upper endpoint of the rescaled time interval. The limiting rescaled meridional field is therefore bounded, with vanishing azimuthal vorticity and vanishing divergence; hence its gradient vanishes, which contradicts the selection of the points at which we zoomed in. The elimination of the circulation first, and of the potential vorticity second, is also the mechanism of the Euler rigidity theorem in [13, Theorem 4.5]; what [14] adds is that this argument survives the passage to an ancient limit, in which the transporting field is only a weak-∗* limit.

The anisotropy inherent in the lengths (1.10) forces the proof in this paper to depart from [14]. To see this, note that after the zoom-in, the radial diffusion coefficient is (−t)/ℓr​(t)2=1(-t)/\ell_{r}(t)^{2}=1, the axial one is (−t)/ℓz​(t)2=(−t)2​h(-t)/\ell_{z}(t)^{2}=(-t)^{2h}, and the rescaling multiplies the circulation by (−t)/(ℓr​(t)​ℓz​(t))=(−t)h(-t)/(\ell_{r}(t)\ell_{z}(t))=(-t)^{h}. In the isotropic case all three of these quantities are of size (−t)/ℓ​(t)2→0(-t)/\ell(t)^{2}\to 0 as t↑0t\uparrow 0, and thus all three terms vanish in the zoom-in limit. Here the last two vanish, but the first one does not. The first difficulty is therefore that radial diffusion survives in the limit, which is no longer governed by a transport equation: the step which eliminates the potential vorticity in [13, 14], its conservation along backward meridional trajectories, is unavailable. In place of an argument based on backward characteristics, we use Lemma 3.3, which is a comparison principle for bounded distributional solutions of a drift-diffusion equation whose diffusion acts in a (strict) subset of the variables.

As in [14], the zoom-in limit need not be a solution of (1.2), so we take the curl of (1.2) first, which removes the pressure, and carry only the vorticity equations (3.3) and (3.4) into the limit. Whether the rescaled axis stays at finite distance or recedes, the limiting scalar is bounded, solves a homogeneous equation on the whole space, and tends uniformly to zero in the remote past; the comparison principle then implies that it vanishes. Incompressibility and the boundedness of the limiting velocity then give smallness of (−t)​∂rur(-t)\partial_{r}u_{r} and (−t)​∂zuz(-t)\partial_{z}u_{z}, and, when the rescaled axis stays at finite distance, of (−t)​ur/r(-t)u_{r}/r; when it recedes, that quotient is small by (1.11) alone. Lastly, the bound (−t)​|∂zur|≤C​(−t)h(-t)|\partial_{z}u_{r}|\leq C(-t)^{h} is immediate from (1.11), and it gives the relative smallness of this term as well.

The second difficulty is that ∂ruz\partial_{r}u_{z} may be as large as C​(−t)−1−hC(-t)^{-1-h}, so that an o⁡((−t)−1)o((-t)^{-1}) bound on the full gradient of the meridional velocity b=ur​er+uz​ezb=u_{r}e_{r}+u_{z}e_{z} is unavailable at any stage of the argument. We therefore track only the four quantities in

(1.12) Gρ​(t):=‖|∂rur​(⋅,t)|+|ur​(⋅,t)/r|+|∂zuz​(⋅,t)|+|∂zur​(⋅,t)|‖L∞​(B​(ρ)),\displaystyle G_{\rho}(t):=\bigl\||\partial_{r}u_{r}(\cdot,t)|+|u_{r}(\cdot,t)/r|+|\partial_{z}u_{z}(\cdot,t)|+|\partial_{z}u_{r}(\cdot,t)|\bigr\|_{L^{\infty}(B(\rho))}\,,

where ur/ru_{r}/r is extended continuously across the axis. The second quantity is dominated by the first in the supremum over B⁡(ρ)B(\rho), since uru_{r} vanishes on the axis and the radial segment to the axis stays in B⁡(ρ)B(\rho); we keep it because Section 5 uses ur/ru_{r}/r as the coefficient of uθu_{\theta} in (3.1c) and of ωθ2\omega_{\theta}^{2} in (5.7). The relative smallness result, which replaces [14, Proposition 3.1], is as follows:

Proposition 1.5 (Smallness of the meridional quantities).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.3, for every fixed 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 we have

(1.13) limt↑0(−t)​Gρ​(t)=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\uparrow 0}(-t)G_{\rho}(t)=0\,.

To deduce regularity at (0,0)(0,0) from (1.13), we first show that for every η>0\eta>0 the bound ‖uθ​(⋅,t)‖L∞≤Cη​(−t)−η\|u_{\theta}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{\eta}(-t)^{-\eta} holds on an interior ball, at all sufficiently late times; we obtain this bound by applying the maximum principle in the swirl equation to the function (−t)η​uθ(-t)^{\eta}u_{\theta}. We then consider the local enstrophy balance, which contains the nonlinear term (∂ruz)​ωr​ωz(\partial_{r}u_{z})\omega_{r}\omega_{z}, whose coefficient ∂ruz\partial_{r}u_{z} may be of size (−t)−1−h(-t)^{-1-h}, too large to be placed in L∞L^{\infty} and fed to Grönwall’s inequality. Appealing instead to the identity ωr=−∂zuθ\omega_{r}=-\partial_{z}u_{\theta}, we integrate by parts in zz, which moves the derivative from the swirl onto the product (∂ruz)​ωz(\partial_{r}u_{z})\omega_{z}. As a consequence, the swirl enters only through its supremum, and the two factors of the product are controlled by the enstrophy and the enstrophy dissipation through local div-curl estimates. The resulting enstrophy estimate then closes and gives a Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin bound up to time zero, as we show in Section 5.

1.5. Prior results on axisymmetric Navier-Stokes

Without swirl, axisymmetric solutions of 3D Navier-Stokes are globally regular; see Ladyzhenskaya [36] and also Ukhovskii and Yudovich [62]. With swirl, the global regularity question is open and only conditional results are available. Singularities which obey a scale-invariant (so-called Type I) pointwise bound are excluded: |u|≤C(r2−t)−1/2|u|\leq C(r^{2}-t)^{-1/2} by Chen, Strain, Yau, and Tsai [7]; r​|u|≤Cr|u|\leq C by Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin, and Šverák [33], and |u|≤C(−t)−1/2|u|\leq C(-t)^{-1/2} by Chen, Strain, Tsai, and Yau [8]. Seregin and Šverák [54] proved a local Type I regularity criterion which imposes the bound ≤C(−t)−1/2\leq C(-t)^{-1/2} only on the meridional part of the velocity. For a detailed account of the many other conditional results available for axisymmetric Navier-Stokes, we refer to the book of Tsai [61, Chapter 10].

Past the Type I threshold, singularities are constrained by the growth of critical norms: the Lt∞​Lx3L^{\infty}_{t}L^{3}_{x} theorem of Escauriaza, Seregin, and Šverák [24] was made quantitative by Tao [59], and was adapted to the axisymmetric class, with quantitative improvements, by Palasek [46] and by Ożański and Palasek [45].

Closer to the hypotheses of this paper, Seregin [49] showed that an axisymmetric singularity must be of Type II, in the sense of local scale-invariant integral quantities. Moreover, in [50, 51, 52, 53] he reduced the Type II blowup scenario to a Liouville problem for ancient Euler solutions, which may be ruled out in special cases.

1.6. Research context for the OpenAI construction

The problem of spontaneous generation of singularities in incompressible fluids has a long history and a strong scientific motivation. Research in this area has produced a vast literature which forms the fertile environment surrounding the OpenAI construction. We do not have space here to do justice to the numerous ideas and results in this area, but it would not be amiss to mention some of the important developments which are relevant to [43].

For the incompressible 3D Euler equations, Elgindi [22] proved finite time singularity formation for axisymmetric solutions without swirl, with a velocity of class C1,αC^{1,\alpha} for α>0\alpha>0 sufficiently small; see also the finite energy version in Elgindi, Ghoul, and Masmoudi [23]. Earlier this year, blowup constructions in the swirl-free axisymmetric setting were obtained for the entire permissible range α∈(0,1/3)\alpha\in(0,1/3), independently, by Shkoller [57], Chen [10, 11], and Shao, Wei, Zhang, and Zhang [56]. For smooth initial data in the presence of a solid boundary, Chen and Hou [9] proved finite time blowup for 3D Euler using modulated self-similar analysis and a computer-assisted argument. Closer to the Navier-Stokes equations, Tao [58] constructed finite time blowup for an “averaged” Navier-Stokes equation, whose modified nonlinearity retains the scaling and energy structure of the original PDE. Numerical and machine-guided searches for a self-similar blowup profile for 3D Euler and other incompressible fluid models were performed in [29, 30, 63, 64, 26, 21]. These computations have shaped the expectations for a rigorous construction: which scenarios are worth pursuing, and at which regularity a singularity should be looked for. All results mentioned in this paragraph consider the classical, unforced, problem.77 7 We note that recently OpenAI has also claimed to prove finite time blowup for the 3D Euler equations, from smooth compactly supported initial data [44].

A different route to blowup for the 3D Euler equations (and related models), in the presence of a body force, was opened by Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa. The force injects, at a sequence of times accumulating at the blowup time, small perturbations at ever higher frequencies, which the nonlinearity amplifies. The question is then how smooth and how small the force can be made. We refer to [15] for the 3D Euler result, with a force which lies in C1,1/2−ε∩L2C^{1,1/2-\varepsilon}\cap L^{2} uniformly in time, and to [16] for the 2D incompressible porous media result, with a source which is C∞C^{\infty} smooth in space, uniformly in time. In this direction, Alpöge and Buckmaster have reached a force which is C∞C^{\infty} in both space and time. Very recently they announced finite time blowup for the 3D Euler equations [2], for the inviscid 2D Boussinesq system [1], and, with Coiculescu, for the 2D incompressible porous media equation [3]. Each of these three papers considers a Cx,t∞C^{\infty}_{x,t} smooth force.

At the technical level, the OpenAI manuscript names two additional research programs whose ideas have influenced its construction. For the evolution of the wavevectors and of the velocity polarizations of the oscillatory pulses along the background flow, [43] records the methods of Lifschitz and Hameiri [39] and of Friedlander and Vishik [25], which detect the instability of an inviscid flow under short wavelength perturbations. For the realization of a prescribed stress by the addition of high frequency oscillations, [43] records the use of ideas from the convex integration program for incompressible fluid equations, introduced by De Lellis and Székelyhidi [18, 19], and then further developed in [17, 31, 5] and many others.

We emphasize that several decades of conditional regularity results restrict the form that a putative 3D Navier-Stokes singularity may take; this helps tremendously if one tries to narrow the search space for a blowing up solution. For a suitable weak solution whose force is bounded, the partial regularity theory of Caffarelli, Kohn, and Nirenberg [6] forces the singular set to have vanishing one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure. The singularity, moreover, cannot be of the backward self-similar form proposed by Leray, cf. Nečas, Růžička, and Šverák [42] for L3L^{3} profiles, Tsai [60] for LpL^{p} profiles with 3<p<∞3<p<\infty under local energy assumptions, and Pineau and Vicol [48] for rotated self-similar profiles which obey a Type I bound, at small or large rotation speeds. Nor can the direction of the vorticity stay coherent, by the alignment criterion of Constantin and Fefferman [12]. In the axisymmetric class, the Type I bounds recalled in Section 1.5 likewise exclude singularities. Self-similar Euler profiles with similarity exponent below 1/21/2, which is the range that a Navier-Stokes zoom at an Euler length would require, are also excluded when the profile is smooth and satisfies an outgoing property [13]. Note that apart from the partial regularity theory, these results consider the unforced Navier-Stokes problem. The above list is far from being complete; we refer to the book of Lemarié-Rieusset [38] for an excellent recent survey.

Remark 1.6 (Forced singularity constructions for shell models).

Returning to the forced constructions, we draw an analogy with the finite time singularities constructed for model equations motivated by Navier-Stokes. Palasek [47, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.5] recently proved finite time blowup in the energy supercritical range for a viscous shell model of Obukhov type, with super-exponentially separated frequencies. His initial data is smooth, and the smooth force he considers is such that its norms all tend to zero at the blowup time [47, Remark 1.4]. The force is nonzero at every time before the blowup, so it vanishes identically on no time interval ending at the singularity. The force is a residual, as in [43]: here it is the dissipation of each mode, switched off until that mode is activated [47, Section 3.3]. Interestingly, Palasek notes that the force cannot be dropped in the parameter range he associates to three dimensions [47, Remark 1.4 and Section 1.3.2]; this statement is offered without proof, and is attributed to forthcoming work of Looi.

1.7. Organization of the paper

Section 2 proves the analytic symmetry reduction, deduces Theorem 1.1 from Theorem 1.3, and records the consequences for the force. Sections 3–5 prove Theorem 1.3. Appendix A records the properties claimed for the OpenAI construction which enter the hypotheses of our results, and what those results give for it.

2. Reduction to the axisymmetric problem

In this section we deduce Theorem 1.1 from Theorem 1.3. Throughout this section v=𝒫​uv=\mathcal{P}u and w=u−vw=u-v are as in (1.4), 𝒬=B⁡(1)×(−1,0)\mathcal{Q}=B(1)\times(-1,0), and (u,π)(u,\pi) is smooth on compact subsets of the cylinder on which it is given, so that ff is smooth there as well.

2.1. Spatial analyticity at a fixed time before blowup

That u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is real analytic in space at each fixed t<0t<0 is classical. We recall the statement in the form in which it is used here and in Remark 2.6. No analyticity in time is assumed.

Theorem 2.1 (Interior spatial analyticity [32, Theorem 1.2]).

Let R>0R>0, t1<t2t_{1}<t_{2}, and let (u,π)(u,\pi) be a solution of (1.2) on the cylinder B⁡(R)×(t1,t2)B(R)\times(t_{1},t_{2}), smooth on compact subsets of that cylinder. Assume that the force is real analytic in the space variables, locally uniformly on cylinders compactly contained in B⁡(R)×(t1,t2)B(R)\times(t_{1},t_{2}): for every R′<RR^{\prime}<R and every compact interval J⊂(t1,t2)J\subset(t_{1},t_{2}) there are M<∞M<\infty and a>0a>0 such that88 8 Since k!≤kk≤ek​k!k!\leq k^{k}\leq e^{k}k! for k≥1k\geq 1, the hypothesis (2.1) is unchanged if |α|!|\alpha|! is replaced by |α||α||\alpha|^{|\alpha|}, which is the form in which Kahane states it on p. 387 of [32].

(2.1) supt∈J‖∂xαf⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B⁡(R′))≤M​a−|α|​|α|!for all ​α∈ℕ03.\displaystyle\sup_{t\in J}\left\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(R^{\prime}))}\leq Ma^{-|\alpha|}|\alpha|!\qquad\mbox{for all }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{3}\,.

Then, the velocity obeys a bound of the same form: for every R′<RR^{\prime}<R and every compact interval J⊂(t1,t2)J\subset(t_{1},t_{2}) there are M′<∞M^{\prime}<\infty and a′>0a^{\prime}>0 such that

(2.2) supt∈J‖∂xαu⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B⁡(R′))≤M′​(a′)−|α|​|α|!for all ​α∈ℕ03.\displaystyle\sup_{t\in J}\left\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(R^{\prime}))}\leq M^{\prime}(a^{\prime})^{-|\alpha|}|\alpha|!\qquad\mbox{for all }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{3}\,.

In particular, u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is real analytic on B⁡(R)B(R) for every t∈(t1,t2)t\in(t_{1},t_{2}). The constants M′M^{\prime} and a′a^{\prime} depend on R′R^{\prime} and JJ, and they need not be uniform up to the parabolic boundary: a′a^{\prime} may tend to zero as JJ approaches an endpoint of (t1,t2)(t_{1},t_{2}).

For a conservative force this is Kahane’s theorem [32, Theorem 1.2], proved there for weak solutions, under the hypotheses of Serrin’s interior regularity theorem [55, Section 3]. For a nonconservative force, Kahane states on p. 387 of [32] that the conclusion of [32, Theorem 1.2] persists once ff obeys (2.1) in its |α||α||\alpha|^{|\alpha|} form, with analyticity understood as the bound [32, equation (1.5)], which is (2.2) above. The point is not taken up again in that paper, so we indicate why the proof goes through. First, the spatial derivatives are estimated in [32] through the representation formulas of Serrin [55, equations (18) and (20)]. With a force, the heat potential for the vorticity carries ff at order zero, in the slot of the bilinear term [55, Section 4, equation (23) and the display which follows it]. Second, adjoining ff to the unknown (u,ω)(u,\omega) of the abstract integral system of [32, Theorem 1.3] makes the force one more component of the inhomogeneity, in rows whose two kernel blocks vanish. Third, the two hypotheses of that theorem hold: the unknown, now the triple (u,ω,f)(u,\omega,f), is bounded on every compact cylinder, by smoothness here and by [32, Theorem 1.1] in [32]; and the inhomogeneity obeys [32, equation (1.5)], which for ff is the bound (2.1). The inductive estimates of [32, Section 4] then apply without change.

The hypothesis (1.6) of Theorem 1.1 is (2.1) on the unit parabolic cylinder. In this paper we apply Theorem 2.1 in the following form.

Corollary 2.2 (Spatial analyticity at a fixed time before blowup).

Let R,δ>0R,\delta>0, and let (u,π)(u,\pi) be a solution of (1.2) on B⁡(R)×(−δ,0)B(R)\times(-\delta,0), smooth on compact subsets of that cylinder. Suppose that for some 0<R′≤R0<R^{\prime}\leq R, some −δ<t1<t2<0-\delta<t_{1}<t_{2}<0, and some M<∞M<\infty and a>0a>0,

(2.3) supt∈[t1,t2]‖∂xαf⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(B⁡(R′))≤M​a−|α|​|α|!for all ​α∈ℕ03.\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[t_{1},t_{2}]}\left\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(R^{\prime}))}\leq Ma^{-|\alpha|}|\alpha|!\qquad\mbox{for all }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{3}\,.

Then, for every t∈(t1,t2)t\in(t_{1},t_{2}), the velocity u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is real analytic on B⁡(R′)B(R^{\prime}).

This is Theorem 2.1 on the cylinder B⁡(R′)×(t1,t2)B(R^{\prime})\times(t_{1},t_{2}), on which (2.3) gives (2.1) with the same MM and aa. Since the zero force satisfies (2.3) on every cylinder, for the unforced equations u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is real analytic on B⁡(R)B(R) at every t∈(−δ,0)t\in(-\delta,0).

We note that analyticity in space and time for the Navier-Stokes equations was proved by Masuda [41]; this result was extended to uniform analyticity up to an analytic boundary by Komatsu [34]. Quantitative lower bounds on the radius of spatial analyticity are due to Grujić and Kukavica [27], in terms of LpL^{p} norms of the initial datum. At interior points, and for a divergence-free force analytic on a ball, this result is due to Bradshaw, Grujić, and Kukavica [4].

2.3. Consequences for the force

The analyticity of the force enters the proof of Theorem 1.1 at exactly one point, the passage from symmetry on the shrinking core (1.8), to the symmetry (2.5) on the fixed ball; for a merely smooth force we do not know how to make that passage. At a singular point, we may restate Theorem 1.1 as a statement about the force alone.

Corollary 2.3 (The force under an axisymmetric core).

Let (u,π)(u,\pi) be a suitable weak solution of (1.2) on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, smooth on compact subsets of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, with a force ff satisfying (1.5), assume (1.7) for some 0<h<1/20<h<1/2 and 𝖢axi<∞\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}<\infty, and assume (1.8). If (0,0)(0,0) is a singular point, then ff violates (1.6), and in particular f≢0f\not\equiv 0 there. Moreover, ff then does not vanish identically on any cylinder B⁡(R′)×(−δ′,0)B(R^{\prime})\times(-\delta^{\prime},0) with 0<R′≤10<R^{\prime}\leq 1 and 0<δ′≤10<\delta^{\prime}\leq 1.

Proof of Corollary 2.3.

The first assertion is the contrapositive of Theorem 1.1, and f=0f=0 satisfies (1.6). For the second, were ff to vanish identically on such a cylinder, the hypotheses of Theorem 1.1 would hold there with ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) replaced by min⁡{ρ⁡(t),R′/2}\min\{\rho(t),R^{\prime}/2\}, and the Navier-Stokes scaling would make (0,0)(0,0) regular. ∎

Remark 2.4 (Upper bounds in place of exact vanishing).

We note that exact axisymmetry on the core may be replaced by a bound on the non-axisymmetric part ww of the velocity, on a fixed ball. That is, if in Theorem 1.1 we drop (1.8) and (1.6) and assume instead that

(2.6) Mw:=sup−1<t<0‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖Cx3​(B​(1))<∞,\displaystyle M_{w}:=\sup_{-1<t<0}\left\|w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{C_{x}^{3}(B(1))}<\infty\,,

then (0,0)(0,0) is still regular. No smallness of MwM_{w} is required, and analyticity plays no role. Indeed, averaging (1.2) over rotations kills the mixed terms (v⋅∇)w(v\cdot\nabla)w and (w⋅∇)v(w\cdot\nabla)v, since vv is invariant and 𝒫​w=0\mathcal{P}w=0, and gives

(2.7a) ∂tv+(v⋅∇)v−Δv+∇π¯\displaystyle\partial_{t}v+(v\cdot\nabla)v-\Delta v+\nabla\bar{\pi} =F+f¯,\displaystyle=F+\bar{f}\,,
(2.7b) div⁡v\displaystyle\operatorname{div}v =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
(2.7c) F\displaystyle F =−𝒫((w⋅∇)w),\displaystyle=-\mathcal{P}\bigl((w\cdot\nabla)w\bigr)\,,
(2.7d) sup−1<t<0‖F⁡(⋅,t)‖Cx2​(B​(1))\displaystyle\sup_{-1<t<0}\left\|F(\cdot,t)\right\|_{C_{x}^{2}(B(1))} ≤C​Mw2,\displaystyle\leq CM_{w}^{2}\,,

where CC is a universal constant, and f¯=𝒫​f\bar{f}=\mathcal{P}f. Averaging does not increase the norms in (1.3), and (v,π¯)(v,\bar{\pi}) is smooth on compact subsets of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, so it is a suitable weak solution of (2.7) with the force F+f¯F+\bar{f}, whose C2C^{2} norm is at most C​Mw2+C​MfCM_{w}^{2}+CM_{f}. Theorem 1.3 makes vv bounded near (0,0)(0,0), and (2.6) makes u=v+wu=v+w bounded there as well. We emphasize that the identity theorem uses the exact vanishing in (1.8), and that we do not know how to replace it by an algebraic rate of smallness. Section A.6 shows that (2.6) fails for the OpenAI construction.

Remark 2.5 (The symmetry of the curl of the force).

No symmetry of ff is assumed in Theorem 1.1, but the hypotheses (1.8) and (1.6) together imply one: for every φ∈[0,2​π)\varphi\in[0,2\pi),

(2.8) ℛφ​(curl⁡f)=curl⁡f,on ​𝒬.\displaystyle\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}(\operatorname{curl}f)=\operatorname{curl}f\,,\qquad\mbox{on }\mathcal{Q}\,.

Indeed, once ℛφ​u=u\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}u=u is known from the proof of Theorem 1.1, applying ℛφ\mathscr{R}_{\varphi} to the momentum equation gives f−ℛφ​f=∇(π−π∘Qφ−1)f-\mathscr{R}_{\varphi}f=\nabla(\pi-\pi\circ Q_{\varphi}^{-1}), and (2.8) follows upon taking the curl. It would be interesting to decide whether in Theorem 1.1 assumption (1.6) may be replaced by the rotation invariance (2.8) of curl⁡f\operatorname{curl}f.

Remark 2.6 (Exterior vanishing and analyticity).

A second obstruction to the analyticity of the force uses neither (1.7) nor (1.8), only an open set off the axis on which the meridional velocity vanishes. Let (u,π)(u,\pi) be a solution of (1.2) on B⁡(R)×(−δ,0)B(R)\times(-\delta,0), smooth on compact subsets of that cylinder, and let E⊂B(R)∩{r>0}E\subset B(R)\cap\{r>0\} be a nonempty open set such that

(2.9) ur=uz=0on ​E×(−δ,0).\displaystyle u_{r}=u_{z}=0\qquad\mbox{on }E\times(-\delta,0)\,.

Suppose that uz​(0,t0)≠0u_{z}(0,t_{0})\neq 0 for some t0∈(−δ,0)t_{0}\in(-\delta,0).99 9 For the OpenAI construction this holds at every time sufficiently close to the blowup time, where uz(0,t)=j0(−t)−1/2−h≠0u_{z}(0,t)=j_{0}(-t)^{-1/2-h}\neq 0 by (A.12). The remark thus says that a flow which is pure swirl on an open set off the axis, and has nonzero axial velocity at a point of the axis, cannot arise from a spatially analytic force: analyticity would carry the exterior vanishing of uzu_{z} to the axis. Then, on every ball B⁡(R′)B(R^{\prime}) with 0<R′≤R0<R^{\prime}\leq R which meets EE, and for every t1∈(−δ,t0)t_{1}\in(-\delta,t_{0}), there are no constants M<∞M<\infty and a>0a>0 such that

In particular, ff does not vanish identically on B⁡(R′)×(t1,t0)B(R^{\prime})\times(t_{1},t_{0}), since the zero force satisfies (2.10). The proof is short. Suppose that (2.10) holds for some MM and aa. By Corollary 2.2, u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is then real analytic on B⁡(R′)B(R^{\prime}) for every t∈(t1,t0)t\in(t_{1},t_{0}). At each such tt, the scalar uz​(⋅,t)u_{z}(\cdot,t) vanishes on the nonempty open set E∩B⁡(R′)E\cap B(R^{\prime}) by (2.9), hence on all of B⁡(R′)B(R^{\prime}) by the identity theorem, and in particular uz​(0,t)=0u_{z}(0,t)=0. Letting t↑t0t\uparrow t_{0} and using the continuity of uz​(0,⋅)u_{z}(0,\cdot), we obtain uz​(0,t0)=0u_{z}(0,t_{0})=0, a contradiction.

3. Axisymmetric identities and auxiliary results

We now turn to the proof of Theorem 1.3. Throughout Sections 3–5, (u,π)(u,\pi) is an axisymmetric suitable weak solution of (1.2) on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, in the class of Section 1.4, with a force satisfying (1.5); averaging over rotations as in Section 2.2, we may (and do) take π\pi and ff axisymmetric as well. This section records a few of the auxiliary results that the proof needs: the equations in cylindrical variables, a maximum principle for functions vanishing on the axis (Lemma 3.1), a regular annulus with a bounded circulation (Lemma 3.2), and a comparison principle for the bounded scalars produced by the ancient limits of Section 4 (Lemma 3.3). Apart from the force, the identities and Lemma 3.2 are the same as those of the companion paper [14]; the force enters as (curl⁡f)θ(\operatorname{curl}f)_{\theta} in (3.3), as g=(curl⁡f)θ/rg=(\operatorname{curl}f)_{\theta}/r in (3.4), and as r​fθrf_{\theta} in (3.5), and (1.5) bounds all three. We denote by CC a constant which may depend on hh, MfM_{f}, the constant 𝖢axi\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}} of (1.11), and fixed interior radii, but never on a sequence of rescaling times.

3.2. A maximum principle for functions vanishing on the axis

The swirl equation (3.1c) and the circulation equation (3.5) have coefficients which are singular on the axis, and, unlike (3.4), they are not lifted to a higher dimension. The proofs of Lemmas 3.2 and 5.1, and Remark 5.2, apply the maximum principle to them in the following form.

Lemma 3.1 (Maximum principle for functions vanishing on the axis).

Let R>0R>0, t1<st_{1}<s, k∈ℝk\in\mathbb{R}, and M≥0M\geq 0, and define the set D={(x,t):x∈B(R),r=|x′|>0,t1<t≤s}D=\{(x,t)\colon x\in B(R),\ r=|x^{\prime}|>0,\ t_{1}<t\leq s\}. Let ϕ=ϕ⁡(r,z,t)\phi=\phi(r,z,t) be continuous on B⁡(R)¯×[t1,s]\overline{B(R)}\times[t_{1},s], with ϕ⁡(0,z,t)=0\phi(0,z,t)=0 for |z|≤R|z|\leq R and t1≤t≤st_{1}\leq t\leq s. Assume that ϕ\phi is of class C2C^{2} in xx and C1C^{1} in tt on DD, and satisfies

(3.7) ∂tϕ+br∂rϕ+bz∂zϕ+γϕ=(∂r2+kr∂r+∂z2)ϕ+F,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi+b_{r}\partial_{r}\phi+b_{z}\partial_{z}\phi+\gamma\phi=\Bigl(\partial_{r}^{2}+\frac{k}{r}\partial_{r}+\partial_{z}^{2}\Bigr)\phi+F\,,

there. Here brb_{r}, bzb_{z}, γ\gamma, and FF are real-valued functions on DD, with γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 and |F|≤M|F|\leq M; no bound is assumed on brb_{r}, bzb_{z}, or γ\gamma, which may be unbounded as r→0r\to 0. Then

(3.8) |ϕ⁡(x,t)|≤maxΣ⁡|ϕ|+M⁡(t−t1)on ​B⁡(R)¯×[t1,s],\displaystyle|\phi(x,t)|\leq\max_{\Sigma}|\phi|+M(t-t_{1})\qquad\mbox{on }\overline{B(R)}\times[t_{1},s]\,,

where Σ=(B⁡(R)¯×{t1})∪(∂B⁡(R)×[t1,s])\Sigma=\bigl(\overline{B(R)}\times\{t_{1}\}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\partial B(R)\times[t_{1},s]\bigr) is the parabolic boundary of B⁡(R)×(t1,s]B(R)\times(t_{1},s].

The proof of this lemma is elementary; we present it for the convenience of the reader.

Proof of Lemma 3.1.

Since −ϕ-\phi satisfies the same assumptions, with −F-F in place of FF, it suffices to bound ϕ\phi from above. Let m=maxΣ⁡|ϕ|≥0m=\max_{\Sigma}|\phi|\geq 0 and ε>0\varepsilon>0. 3.3. The regular annulus

Lemma 3.2 below is used twice in the proof of Theorem 1.3: its circulation bound (3.9) removes the swirl source in the zoom of Section 4, and its derivative bounds on the annulus, which hold up to the blowup time, control the cutoff errors of the enstrophy estimate of Section 5, which are supported in that annulus.

Lemma 3.2 (A regular annulus and bounded circulation).

Let 0≤R1<R0<10\leq R_{1}<R_{0}<1. There are radii R1<R−<R+<R0R_{1}<R_{-}<R_{+}<R_{0} and a time t0∈(−1,0)t_{0}\in(-1,0) with the following property. The velocity uu, together with ∇u\nabla u and ∇2u\nabla^{2}u, is bounded on the cylindrical annulus {R−<|x|<R+}×(t0,0)\{R_{-}<|x|<R_{+}\}\times(t_{0},0), and, for each R∗∈(R−,R+)R_{*}\in(R_{-},R_{+}), there is a finite constant CΓC_{\Gamma} such that

(3.9) ‖Γ‖L∞​(B⁡(R∗)×(t0,0))≤CΓ.\displaystyle\left\|\Gamma\right\|_{L^{\infty}(B(R_{*})\times(t_{0},0))}\leq C_{\Gamma}\,.
Proof of Lemma 3.2.

3.4. A comparison principle with diffusion in fewer variables

In the ancient limits of Section 4 the radial diffusion survives the zoom-in procedure, so that the potential vorticity is no longer conserved along backward meridional trajectories, as it is in [13] and [14]. A comparison principle is instead used to make the limiting scalar vanish. That scalar, however, is merely bounded, it solves its equation only in the sense of distributions, and it comes with no bound on its derivatives and no initial trace. Moreover, the diffusion acts in a subset of the variables only (it does not act in the axial variable), so Lemma 3.3 is stated in the generality in which it is used.

Lemma 3.3 (Comparison for a bounded distributional solution).

Let 1≤d≤m1\leq d\leq m, let I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} be an open interval, and denote x=(X,Z)∈ℝd×ℝm−dx=(X,Z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{m-d}. (3.10) ΛJ:=ess​supτ∈J⁡(‖B⁡(⋅,τ)‖L∞​(ℝm)+‖∇B​(⋅,τ)‖L∞​(ℝm))<∞,\displaystyle\Lambda_{J}:=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\tau\in J}\big(\left\|B(\cdot,\tau)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})}+\left\|\nabla B(\cdot,\tau)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})}\big)<\infty\,,

for every compact interval J⊂IJ\subset I. Let q∈Lloc∞​(I,L∞​(ℝm))q\in L^{\infty}_{\rm loc}(I;L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})) satisfy

(3.11) ∂τq+B⋅∇q=ΔX​qon ​ℝm×I,\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}q+B\cdot\nabla q=\Delta_{X}q\qquad\mbox{on }\mathbb{R}^{m}\times I\,,

in the sense of distributions.1111 11 Here B⋅∇qB\cdot\nabla q really means div⁡(B​q)−(div⁡B)​q\operatorname{div}(Bq)-(\operatorname{div}B)q. Then, for almost every τ0∈I\tau_{0}\in I and almost every τ∈I\tau\in I with τ>τ0\tau>\tau_{0},

If in addition I=(−∞,T)I=(-\infty,T) and, for some C<∞C<\infty and κ>0\kappa>0,

(3.13) ‖q⁡(⋅,τ)‖L∞​(ℝm)≤C​|τ|−κ,\displaystyle\left\|q(\cdot,\tau)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})}\leq C|\tau|^{-\kappa}\,,

for almost every τ<min⁡{−1,T}\tau<\min\{-1,T\}, then q=0q=0 almost everywhere on ℝm×I\mathbb{R}^{m}\times I. A continuous representative of qq on an open subset vanishes there, and so does any continuous trace at the upper endpoint obtained from that representative.

Proof of Lemma 3.3.

The argument is standard: we mollify in space, control the commutator as in [20], and compare with a barrier which grows linearly at infinity. We fix a compact interval J=[τ−,τ+]⊂IJ=[\tau_{-},\tau_{+}]\subset I, set M∞=‖q‖L∞​(ℝm×J)M_{\infty}=\|q\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m}\times J)}, and mollify in space, qε=ηε∗qq_{\varepsilon}=\eta_{\varepsilon}*q with a standard mollifier ηε=ε−mη(⋅/ε)\eta_{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon^{-m}\eta(\cdot/\varepsilon) with η\eta supported in B⁡(1)B(1). Convolving (3.11) with ηε\eta_{\varepsilon}, we obtain

(3.14) ∂τqε+B⋅∇qε=ΔX​qε+ℛε,ℛε=B⋅∇(ηε∗q)−ηε∗(B⋅∇q).\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}q_{\varepsilon}+B\cdot\nabla q_{\varepsilon}=\Delta_{X}q_{\varepsilon}+\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\,,\qquad\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}=B\cdot\nabla(\eta_{\varepsilon}*q)-\eta_{\varepsilon}*(B\cdot\nabla q)\,.

Here ℛε\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon} is the commutator of DiPerna and Lions, bounded in the usual way: |ℛε|≤C⁡(m,η)​ΛJ​M∞|\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}|\leq C(m,\eta)\Lambda_{J}M_{\infty} by (3.10). Moreover, ℛε​(⋅,τ)→0\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(\cdot,\tau)\to 0 in Lloc2​(ℝm)L^{2}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{m}) for almost every τ∈J\tau\in J by [20, Lemma II.1], hence ℛε→0\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\to 0 in L2​(B​(R)×J)L^{2}(B(R)\times J) for every R>0R>0 by dominated convergence. For a fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, every term of (3.14) other than ∂τqε\partial_{\tau}q_{\varepsilon} is bounded, so qεq_{\varepsilon} has a representative which is Lipschitz in time with values in L∞​(ℝm)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m}); from now on qεq_{\varepsilon} denotes this representative. If τ0\tau_{0} is a Lebesgue point of τ↦q⁡(⋅,τ)∈Lloc1​(ℝm)\tau\mapsto q(\cdot,\tau)\in L^{1}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{m}), which is the case for almost every τ0\tau_{0}, then qε​(⋅,τ0)=ηε∗q⁡(⋅,τ0)q_{\varepsilon}(\cdot,\tau_{0})=\eta_{\varepsilon}*q(\cdot,\tau_{0}) for every ε\varepsilon. We fix such a τ0∈(τ−,τ+)\tau_{0}\in(\tau_{-},\tau_{+}) and set M=‖q⁡(⋅,τ0)‖L∞​(ℝm)M=\|q(\cdot,\tau_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})}, so that qε​(⋅,τ0)≤Mq_{\varepsilon}(\cdot,\tau_{0})\leq M.

With ⟨x⟩=(1+|x|2)1/2\langle x\rangle=(1+|x|^{2})^{1/2} we have |∇⟨x⟩|≤1|\nabla\langle x\rangle|\leq 1 and ΔX​⟨x⟩≤d\Delta_{X}\langle x\rangle\leq d. Upon defining K=ΛJ+dK=\Lambda_{J}+d, the function

(3.15) Ψσ​(x,τ)=M+σ⁡(⟨x⟩+K⁡(τ−τ0)),σ>0,\displaystyle\Psi_{\sigma}(x,\tau)=M+\sigma\big(\langle x\rangle+K(\tau-\tau_{0})\big)\,,\qquad\sigma>0\,,

satisfies ∂τΨσ+B⋅∇Ψσ−ΔX​Ψσ≥σ⁡(K−ΛJ−d)=0\partial_{\tau}\Psi_{\sigma}+B\cdot\nabla\Psi_{\sigma}-\Delta_{X}\Psi_{\sigma}\geq\sigma(K-\Lambda_{J}-d)=0 almost everywhere on ℝm×J\mathbb{R}^{m}\times J, and Ψσ≥M+σ​|x|\Psi_{\sigma}\geq M+\sigma|x| for τ≥τ0\tau\geq\tau_{0}. Hence vε=(qε−Ψσ)+v_{\varepsilon}=(q_{\varepsilon}-\Psi_{\sigma})_{+} vanishes at τ=τ0\tau=\tau_{0}; for τ∈[τ0,τ+]\tau\in[\tau_{0},\tau_{+}] it also vanishes on the complement of B⁡(Rσ)B(R_{\sigma}) for Rσ=1+M∞/σR_{\sigma}=1+M_{\infty}/\sigma. Subtracting the supersolution inequality from (3.14), multiplying by vεv_{\varepsilon}, and integrating over ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, we obtain

(3.16) 12​dd​τ​∫vε2+∫|∇Xvε|2≤12​∫(div⁡B)​vε2+∫ℛε​vε.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{d\tau}\int v_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\int|\nabla_{X}v_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}\int(\operatorname{div}B)v_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\int\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}v_{\varepsilon}\,.

Appealing to Grönwall’s inequality we obtain supτ∈[τ0,τ+]‖vε​(⋅,τ)‖L22≤CJ​‖ℛε‖L2​(B⁡(Rσ)×J)2→0\sup_{\tau\in[\tau_{0},\tau_{+}]}\|v_{\varepsilon}(\cdot,\tau)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq C_{J}\|\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(B(R_{\sigma})\times J)}^{2}\to 0 as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0. Since qε→qq_{\varepsilon}\to q in Lloc2L^{2}_{\rm loc}, letting ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 and then σ↓0\sigma\downarrow 0 gives q≤Mq\leq M almost everywhere on ℝm×(τ0,τ+)\mathbb{R}^{m}\times(\tau_{0},\tau_{+}). The same argument for −q-q, and an exhaustion of II by compact intervals, give (3.12).

For the last assertion, we apply (3.12) at times τj→−∞\tau_{j}\to-\infty at which (3.13) holds, and obtain ‖q⁡(⋅,τ)‖L∞​(ℝm)≤C​|τj|−κ\|q(\cdot,\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})}\leq C|\tau_{j}|^{-\kappa} for almost every τ>τj\tau>\tau_{j}; thus q=0q=0 almost everywhere, and a continuous representative, together with its trace at the upper endpoint, vanishes identically. ∎

4. Ancient limits and smallness of the meridional quantities

The goal of this section is to prove Proposition 1.5. We argue by contradiction, zooming in where (1.13) fails, at the radial length ℓr\ell_{r} and the axial length ℓz\ell_{z}. Two cases then arise, according to whether the rescaled axis stays at finite distance, or recedes to infinity. Since the pressure is not controlled after the zoom, we pass to the limit in the vorticity equations (3.3) and (3.4), not in the momentum equation. In both cases the rescaling makes the bounded circulation subcritical, and this removes the swirl source. The radial diffusion, however, survives the rescaling, so that the limiting vorticity vanishes by the comparison principle of Lemma 3.3, not by transport along characteristics. Incompressibility and the boundedness of the limiting meridional velocity then make the selected quantities vanish in the limit, and this contradicts the choice of the points at which we zoom in.

Proof of Proposition 1.5.

Fix an arbitrary 0<ρ<10<\rho<1. By (1.11) the fourth term in (1.12) is bounded as (−t)​|∂zur|≤𝖢axi​(−t)h(-t)|\partial_{z}u_{r}|\leq\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}(-t)^{h}, and thus tends to zero in the limit.

Suppose by contradiction that (1.13) fails. Then there exist c0>0c_{0}>0, times tn↑0t_{n}\uparrow 0, and points xn∈B⁡(ρ)x_{n}\in B(\rho) at which the other three terms satisfy

(4.1) (−tn)​(|∂rur|+|urr|+|∂zuz|)​(xn,tn)≥c0.\displaystyle(-t_{n})\Bigl(|\partial_{r}u_{r}|+\Bigl|\frac{u_{r}}{r}\Bigr|+|\partial_{z}u_{z}|\Bigr)(x_{n},t_{n})\geq c_{0}\,.

By rotation invariance we may without loss of generality take xn=(rn,0,zn)x_{n}=(r_{n},0,z_{n}), where rn=|xn′|≥0r_{n}=|x_{n}^{\prime}|\geq 0. By Lemma 3.2, applied with R1=ρR_{1}=\rho and some R0∈(ρ,1)R_{0}\in(\rho,1), there are ρ<R∗<1\rho<R_{*}<1, t∗∈(−1,0)t_{*}\in(-1,0), and CΓ<∞C_{\Gamma}<\infty such that

(4.2) |r​uθ​(x,t)|≤CΓonB⁡(R∗)×(t∗,0).\displaystyle|ru_{\theta}(x,t)|\leq C_{\Gamma}\qquad\mbox{on}\qquad B(R_{*})\times(t_{*},0)\,.

Throughout the proof, CC denotes a constant which may depend on hh, MfM_{f}, 𝖢axi\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}, ρ\rho, R∗R_{*}, CΓC_{\Gamma}, and on the compact time interval under consideration, but never on nn.

Step 1: the rescaling. We define

(4.3) λn=(−tn)1/2,δn=(−tn)h=λn2​h,μn=λnδn=(−tn)1/2−h=λn1−2​h.\displaystyle\lambda_{n}=(-t_{n})^{1/2}\,,\qquad\delta_{n}=(-t_{n})^{h}=\lambda_{n}^{2h}\,,\qquad\mu_{n}=\frac{\lambda_{n}}{\delta_{n}}=(-t_{n})^{1/2-h}=\lambda_{n}^{1-2h}\,.

That is, λn=ℓr​(tn)\lambda_{n}=\ell_{r}(t_{n}) and μn=ℓz​(tn)\mu_{n}=\ell_{z}(t_{n}) are the lengths (1.10), and both vanish as n→∞n\to\infty since 0<h<1/20<h<1/2. Their ratio is δn=λn/μn→0\delta_{n}=\lambda_{n}/\mu_{n}\to 0. Upon passing to a subsequence, we have that rn/λnr_{n}/\lambda_{n} either stays bounded or tends to infinity. Every subsequence extracted in this proof refines the previous ones, and we do not relabel it; since (4.1) holds for every nn, it holds along every subsequence. We first zoom in about the point (0,zn)(0,z_{n}) on the axis, in the variables

(4.4) R=rλn,Z=z−znμn,τ=t(−tn),\displaystyle R=\frac{r}{\lambda_{n}}\,,\qquad Z=\frac{z-z_{n}}{\mu_{n}}\,,\qquad\tau=\frac{t}{(-t_{n})}\,,

so that τ=−1\tau=-1 is the selected time tnt_{n} and τ≤−1\tau\leq-1 is its past. We then define

(4.5c) Sn​(R,Z,τ)\displaystyle S_{n}(R,Z,\tau) =λn​δn​uθ​(λn​R,zn+μn​Z,(−tn)​τ),\displaystyle=\lambda_{n}\delta_{n}\,u_{\theta}\bigl(\lambda_{n}R,\,z_{n}+\mu_{n}Z,\,(-t_{n})\tau\bigr)\,,
(4.5d) Ωn​(R,Z,τ)\displaystyle\Omega_{n}(R,Z,\tau) =λn3​δn​Ω​(λn​R,zn+μn​Z,(−tn)​τ),\displaystyle=\lambda_{n}^{3}\delta_{n}\,\Omega\bigl(\lambda_{n}R,\,z_{n}+\mu_{n}Z,\,(-t_{n})\tau\bigr)\,,

where the cylindrical components on the right are written as functions of (r,z,t)(r,z,t). In these variables the bounds (1.11) read as

(4.6a) |∂Ra∂ZbVn|\displaystyle|\partial_{R}^{a}\partial_{Z}^{b}V_{n}| ≤𝖢axi|τ|−(1+a)/2−(1/2−h)b,\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{axi}}|\tau|^{-(1+a)/2-(1/2-h)b}\,,

for all a+b≤2a+b\leq 2.

Since the lengths (4.3) vanish and |zn|<ρ<R∗|z_{n}|<\rho<R_{*}, both preimages contain any given compact subset of [0,∞)×ℝ×(−∞,0)[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\times(-\infty,0) for all nn large depending on that subset.

Since ∂ZVn\partial_{Z}V_{n} and ∂RWn\partial_{R}W_{n} vanish at R=0R=0, as ∂zur\partial_{z}u_{r} and ∂ruz\partial_{r}u_{z} do on the axis (Section 3.1), the quotients ∂ZVn/R\partial_{Z}V_{n}/R and ∂RWn/R\partial_{R}W_{n}/R are bounded by the suprema of ∂R​ZVn\partial_{RZ}V_{n} and ∂R​RWn\partial_{RR}W_{n} on the radial segment which joins (0,Z,τ)(0,Z,\tau) to (R,Z,τ)(R,Z,\tau); this segment again lies in the preimage of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, since B⁡(1)B(1) is convex.
